statement: C.W.M. Hart and Arnold R. Pilling, The Tiwi of North Australia (Holt, Rinehart and Winston, 1960), based on Hart's 1928-29 fieldwork, centered senior men's authority via bride-provision and described a system in which women were largely transacted, with little documented agency or voice. Jane C. Goodale, Tiwi Wives: A Study of the Women of Melville Island, North Australia (University of Washington Press, 1971), based on ~10 months of 1954 fieldwork, presented a direct corrective: women as active strategists who understood and worked the marriage-arrangement system on their own behalf, a documented parallel female initiation cycle omitted from the earlier account, and (in her 1996 "Taramaguti Today," Pacific Studies 19(4)) senior wives as real household-economic managers. Later editions of Hart and Pilling's own book (a third edition, 1988) added Goodale as a contributing co-author — a "corrective-by-incorporation" pattern distinct from the Warlpiri Meggitt-then-Bell case (where the corrective remained a separate, standalone publication) documented elsewhere in this batch; the two should not be treated as structurally identical.
